projectDesc.p: La Colección de Textos Clásicos Europeos (CTCE) supone la creación de una base de datos de Teatro canónico clásico europeo en diferentes idiomas, versiones y refundiciones, todas ellas hipervinculadas.

editorialDecl.p: Las presentes ediciones digitales están basadas, en su mayor parte, en ediciones científicas de reconocido prestigio y se ha tratado, en la mayoría de ocasiones, de respetar sus criterios de edición. Solo en casos muy puntuales el editor digital ha introducido leves cambios de los que da cumplida cuenta en el apartado de "Notas".

div.head: Note on this digital edition
div.p: With the support of research project GVAICO2016-094, funded by Generalitat Valenciana (2016-2017).

For this digital edition, the following alerations have been made with respect to Brooke and Paradise’s edition: the play’s title has be modernized as <<The Old Wife’s Tale>> ; speech prefixes have been expanded, as has the name “ <<Huan.>> ” in a stage direction on page 32; the speech prefix “[ <<Voice>> .]” at line 910 (page 35) has been corrected to “[2 <<Voice>> .]” in order to avoid the repetion of “ <<Voice>> .” in line 905.

castItem.roleDesc: the Old Man at the Cross
a Wandering Knight, in love with Delia
Daughter of the King of Thessaly

sp.speaker: Antic
sp.p: How now, fellow Frolic! What, all amort? Doth this sadness become thy madness? What though we have lost our way in the woods, yet never hang the head as though thou hadst no hope to live till to-morrow; for Fantastic and I will warrant thy life to-night for twenty in the hundred.

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: Antic and Fantastic, as I am frolic franion, never in all my life was I so dead slain. What, to lose our way in the wood, without either fire or candle, so uncomfortable! O cælum! O terra! O Maria! O Neptune!

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: Why makes thou it so strange, seeing Cupid hath led our young master to the fair lady, and she is the only saint that he hath sworn to serve?

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: What resteth, then, but we commit him to his wench, and each of us take his stand up in a tree, and sing out our ill fortune to the tune of " O man in desperation "?

sp.speaker: Antic
sp.p: Desperately spoken, fellow frolic, in the dark; but seeing it falls out thus, let us rehearse the old proverb:

lg.l: "Three merry men, and three merry men,
And three merry men be we;
I in the wood, and thou on the ground,
And Jack sleeps in the tree."

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: Hush! a dog in the wood, or a wooden dog! O comfortable hearing! I had even as lief the chamberlain of the White Horse had called me up to bed.

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: Either hath this trotting cur gone out of his circuit, or else are we near some village, which should not be far off, for I perceive the glimmering of a glow-worm, a candle, or a cat's eye, my life for a halfpenny! Enter [Clunch] a smith, with a lantern and candle In the name of my own father, be thou ox or ass that appearest, tell us what thou art.

sp.speaker: Smith
sp.p: What am I? Why, I am Clunch the smith. What are you? What make you in my territories at this time of the night?

sp.speaker: Antic
sp.p: What do we make, dost thou ask? Why, we make faces for fear; such as if thy mortal eyes could behold, would make thee water the long seams of thy side slops, smith.

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: And, in faith, sir, unless your hospitality do relieve us, we are like to wander, with a sorrowful heigh-ho, among the owlets and hobgoblins of the forest. Good Vulcan, for Cupid's sake that hath cozened us all, befriend us as thou mayst; and command us howsoever, wheresoever, whensoever, in whatsoever, for ever and ever.

sp.speaker: Smith
sp.p: Well, masters, it seems to me you have lost your way in the wood; in consideration whereof, if you will go with Clunch to his cottage, you shall have house-room and a good fire to sit by, although we have no bedding to put you in.

sp.speaker: All
sp.p: O blessed smith, O bountiful Clunch!

sp.speaker: Smith
sp.p: For your further entertainment, it shall be as it may be, so and so. (Here a dog bark.) Hark! this is Ball my dog, that bids you all welcome in his own language. Come, take heed for stumbling on the threshold. – Open door, Madge; take in guests.

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: Welcome, Clunch, and good fellows all, that come with my good man. For my good man's sake, come on, sit down; here is a piece of cheese, and a pudding of my own making.

sp.speaker: Antic
sp.p: Thanks, gammer; a good example for the wives of our town.

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: Gammer, thou and thy good man sit lovingly together; we come to chat, and not to eat.

sp.speaker: Smith
sp.p: Well, masters, if you will eat nothing, take away. Come, what do we to pass away the time? Lay a crab in the fire to roast for lamb's-wool. What, shall we have a game at trump or ruff to drive away the time? How say you?

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: This smith leads a life as merry as a king with Madge his wife. Sirrah Frolic, I am sure thou art not without some round or other; no doubt but Clunch can bear his part.

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: Else think you me ill brought up; so set to it when you will.

lg.l: Whenas the rye reach to the chin,
And chopcherry, chopcherry ripe within,
Strawberries swimming in the cream,
And school-boys playing in the stream;
Then, O, then, O, then, O, my true-love said,
Till that time come again
She could not live a maid.

sp.speaker: Antic
sp.p: This sport does well; but methinks, gammer, a merry winter's tale would drive away the time trimly. Come, I am sure you are not without a score.

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: I' faith, gammer, a tale of an hour long were as good as an hour's sleep.

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: Look you, gammer, of the giant and the king's daughter, and I know not what. I have seen the day, when I was a little one, you might have drawn me a mile after you with such a discourse.

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: Well, since you be so importunate, my good man shall fill the pot and get him to bed; they that ply their work must keep good hours. One of you go lie with him; he is a clean-skinned man, I tell you, without either spavin or wind-gall: so I am content to drive away the time with an old wives' winter's tale.

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: No better hay in Devonshire; o' my word, gammer, I'll be one of your audience.

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: And I another, that's flat.

sp.speaker: Antic
sp.p: Then must I to bed with the good man. – Bonna nox , gammer. – Good night, Frolic.

sp.speaker: Smith
sp.p: Come on, my lad, thou shalt take thy unnatural rest with me.

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: Yet this vantage shall we have of them in the morning, to be ready at the sight thereof extempore.

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: Now this bargain, my masters, must I make with you, that you will say hum and ha to my tale; so shall I know you are awake.

sp.speaker: Both
sp.p: Content, gammer, that will we do.

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: Once upon a time, there was a king, or a lord, or a duke, that had a fair daughter, the fairest that ever was, as white as snow and as red as blood; and once upon a time his daughter was stolen away; and he sent all his men to seek out his daughter; and he sent so long, that he sent all his men out of his land.

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: Who dressed his dinner, then?

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: Nay, either hear my tale, or kiss my tale.

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: Well said! On with your tale, gammer.

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: O Lord, I quite forgot! There was a conjurer, and this conjurer could do any thing, and he turned himself into a great dragon, and carried the king's daughter away in his mouth to a castle that he made of stone; and there he kept her I know not how long, till at last all the king's men went out so long that her two brothers went to seek her. O, I forget! she (he, I would say,) turned a proper young man to a bear in the night, and a man in the day, and keeps by a cross that parts three several ways; and he made his lady run mad – Gods me bones, who comes here?

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: Soft, gammer, here some come to tell your tale for you.

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: Let them alone; let us hear what they will say.

lg.l: Upon these chalky cliffs of Albion
We are arrived now with tedious toil;
And compassing the wide world round about,
To seek our sister, to seek fair Delia forth,
Yet cannot we so much as hear of her.
O fortune cruel, cruel and unkind!
Unkind in that we cannot find our sister,
Our sister, hapless in her cruel chance!
Soft! who have we here?

div1.stage: Enter Senex [Erestus] at the cross, stooping to gather

sp.speaker: 1 Brother
sp.p: Now, father, God be your speed! What do you gather there?

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: Hips and haws, and sticks and straws, and things that I gather on the ground, my son.

sp.speaker: 1 Brother
sp.p: Hips and haws, and sticks and straws! Why, is that all your food, father?

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: Yea, son.

sp.speaker: 2 Brother
sp.p: Father, here is an alms-penny for me; and if I speed in that I go for, I will give thee as good a gown of grey as ever thou diddest wear.

sp.speaker: 1 Brother
sp.p: And, father, here is another alms- penny for me; and if I speed in my journey, I will give thee a palmer's staff of ivory, and a scallop-shell of beaten gold.

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: Was she fair?

sp.speaker: 2 Brother
sp.p: Ay, the fairest for white, and the purest for red, as the blood of the deer, or the driven snow.

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: Then hark well, and mark well, my old spell:

lg.l: Be not afraid of ever stranger;
Start not aside at every danger;
Things that seem are not the same;
Blow a blast at every flame:
For when one flame of fire goes out,
Then comes your wishes well about:
If any ask who told you this good,
Say, the white bear of England's wood.

sp.speaker: 1 Brother
sp.p: Brother, heard you not what the old man said?

lg.l: "Be not afraid of every stranger;
Start not aside for every danger;
Things that seem are not the same;
Blow a blast at every flame;
If any ask who told you this good,
Say, the white bear of England's wood."
Well, if this do us any good,
Well fare the white bear of England's wood!

sp.speaker: Erestus

lg.l: Now sit thee here, and tell a heavy tale,
Sad in thy mood, and sober in thy cheer;
Here sit thee now, and to thyself relate
The hard mishap of thy most wretched state.
In Thessaly I liv'd in sweet content,
Until that fortune wrought my overthrow;
For there I wedded was unto a dame,
That liv'd in honour, virtue, love, and fame.
But Sacrapant, that cursed sorcerer,
Being besotted with my beauteous love,
My dearest love, my true betrothed wife,
Did seek the means to rid me of my life.
But worse than this, he with his chanting spells
Did turn me straight unto an ugly bear;
And when the sun doth settle in the west,
Then I begin to don my ugly hide.
And all the day I sit, as now you see,
And speak in riddles, all inspir'd with rage,
Seeming an old and miserable man,
And yet I am in April of my age.
lg.stage: Enter Venelia his lady, mad; and goes in again.
lg.l: See where Venelia, my betrothed love,
Runs madding, all enrag'd, about the woods,
All by his cursed and enchanting spells. –

sp.stage: Enter Lampriscus with a pot of honey
sp.p: But here comes Lampriscus, my discontented neighbour. How now, neighbour! You look toward the ground as well as I; you muse on something.

sp.speaker: Lampriscus
sp.p: Neighbour, on nothing but on the matter I so often moved to you. If you do anything for charity, help me; if for neighbourhood or brotherhood, help me: never was one so cumbered as is poor Lampriscus; and to begin, I pray receive this pot of honey, to mend your fare.

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: Thanks, neighbour, set it down; honey is always welcome to the bear. And now, neighbour, let me hear the cause of your coming.

sp.speaker: Lampriscus
sp.p: I am, as you know, neighbour, a man unmarried; and lived so unquietly with my two wives, that I keep every year holy the day wherein I buried them both: the first was on Saint Andrew's day, the other on Saint Luke's.

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: And now, neighbour, you of this country say, your custom is out. But on with your tale, neighbour.

sp.speaker: Lampriscus
sp.p: By my first wife, whose tongue wearied me alive, and sounded in my ears like the clapper of a great bell, whose talk was a continual torment to all that dwelt by her or lived nigh her, you have heard me say I had a handsome daughter.

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: True, neighbour.

sp.speaker: Lampriscus
sp.p: She it is that afflicts me with her continual clamours, and hangs on me like a bur. Poor she is, and proud she is; as poor as a sheep new-shorn, and as proud of her hopes as a peacock of her tail well-grown.

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: Well said, Lampriscus! You speak it like an Englishman.

sp.speaker: Lampriscus
sp.p: As curst as a wasp, and as forward as a child new-taken from the mother's teat; she is to my age as smoke to the eyes or as vinegar to the teeth.

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: Holily praised, neighbour. As much for the next.

sp.speaker: Lampriscus
sp.p: By my other wife I had a daughter so hard-favoured, so foul and ill-faced, that I think a grove full of golden trees, and the leaves of rubies and diamonds, would not be a dowry answerable to her deformity.

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: Well, neighbour, now you have spoke, hear me speak. Send them to the well for the water of life; there shall they find their fortunes unlooked for. Neighbour, farewell.

sp.speaker: Lampriscus
sp.p: Farewell, and a thousand! And now goeth poor Lampriscus to put in execution this excellent counsel.

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: Why, this goes round without a fiddling- stick: but, do you hear, gammer, was this the man that was a bear in the night and a man in the day?

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: Ay, this is he; and this man that came to him was a beggar, and dwelt upon a green. But soft! who comes here? O, these are the harvest-men. Ten to one they sing a song of mowing.

div1.stage: Enter the Harvest-men a-singing, with this song double repeated

lg.l: All ye that lovely lovers be,
Pray you for me.
Lo, here we come a-sowing, a-sowing,
And sow sweet fruits of love;
In your sweet hearts well may it prove!

div1.stage: Enter Huanebango with his two-hand sword, and Booby, the clown

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: Gammer, what is he?

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: O, this is one that is going to the conjurer. Let him alone; hear what he says.

sp.speaker: Huanebango
sp.p: Now, by Mars and Mercury, Jupiter and Janus, Sol and Saturnus, Venus and Vesta, Pallas and Proserpina, and by the honour of my house, Polimackeroeplacidus, it is a wonder to see what this love will make silly fellows adventure, even in the wane of their wits and infancy of their discretion. Alas, my friend! what fortune calls thee forth to seek thy fortune among brazen gates, enchanted towers, fire and brimstone, thunder and lightning? Beauty, I tell thee, is peerless, and she precious whom thou affectest. Do off these desires, good countryman; good friend, run away from thyself; and, so soon as thou canst, forget her, whom none must inherit but he that can monsters tame, labours achieve, riddles absolve, loose enchantments, murther magic, and kill conjuring, –and that is the great and mighty Huanebango.

sp.speaker: Booby
sp.p: Hark you, sir, hark you. First know I have here the flurting feather, and have given the parish the start for the long stock: now, sir, if it be no more but running through a little lightning, and thunder, and "riddle me, riddle me what's this?" I'll have the wench from the conjurer, if he were ten conjurers.

sp.speaker: Huanebango
Booby
sp.p: O falsum Latinum! The fair maid is minum , Cum apurtinantibus gibletis and all.

sp.speaker: Huanebango
sp.p: If she be mine, as I assure myself the heavens will do somewhat to reward my worthiness, she shall be allied to none of the meanest gods, but be invested in the most famous stock of Huanebango, – Polimackeroeplacidus my grandfather, my father Pergopolineo, my mother Dionora de Sardinia, famously descended.

sp.speaker: Booby
sp.p: Do you hear, sir? Had not you a cousin that was called Gusteceridis?

sp.speaker: Huanebango
sp.p: Indeed, I had a cousin that sometime followed the court infortunately, and his name Bustegusteceridis.

sp.speaker: Booby
sp.p: O Lord, I know him well! He is the knight of the neat's-feet.

sp.speaker: Huanebango
sp.p: O, he loved no capon better! He hath oftentimes deceived his boy of his dinner; that was his fault, good Bustegusteceridis.

sp.speaker: Booby
sp.p: Come, shall we go along? [Enter Erestus at the cross] Soft! here is an old man at the cross; let us ask him the way thither. – Ho, you gaffer! I pray you tell where the wise man the conjurer dwells.

sp.speaker: Huanebango
sp.p: Where that earthly goddess keepeth her abode, the commander of my thoughts, and fair mistress of my heart.

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: Fair enough, and far enough from thy fingering, son.

sp.speaker: Huanebango
sp.p: I will follow my fortune after mine own fancy, and do according to mine own discretion.

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: Yet give something to an old man before you go.

sp.speaker: Huanebango
sp.p: Father, methinks a piece of this cake might serve your turn.

sp.speaker: Erestus
sp.p: Yea, son.

sp.speaker: Huanebango
sp.p: Huanebango giveth no cakes for alms; ask of them that give gifts for poor beggars. – Fair lady, if thou wert once shrined in this bosom, I would buckler thee haratantara.

sp.speaker: Booby
sp.p: Father, do you see this man? You little think he'll run a mile or two for such a cake, or pass for a pudding. I tell you, father, he has kept such a begging of me for a piece of this cake! Whoo! he comes upon me with "a superfantial substance, and the foison of the earth," that I know not what he means. If he came to me thus, and said, "My friend Booby," or so, why, I could spare him a piece with all my heart; but when he tells me how God hath enriched me above other fellows with a cake, why, he makes me blind and deaf at once. Yet, father, here is a piece of cake for you, as hard as the world goes.

lg.l: Thanks, son, but list to me;
He shall be deaf when thou shalt not see.
Farewell, my son: things may so hit,
Thou mayst have wealth to mend thy wit.

sp.speaker: Booby
sp.p: Farewell, father, farewell; for I must make haste after my two-hand sword that is gone before.

sp.speaker: Sacrapant

lg.l: The day is clear, the welkin bright and grey,
The lark is merry and records her notes;
Each thing rejoiceth underneath the sky,
But only I, whom heaven hath in hate,
Wretched and miserable Sacrapant.
In Thessaly was I born and brought up;
My mother Meroe hight, a famous witch,
And by her cunning I of her did learn
To change and alter shapes of mortal men.
There did I turn myself into a dragon,
And stole away the daughter to the king,
Fair Delia, the mistress of my heart;
And brought her hither to revive the man
That seemeth young and pleasant to behold,
And yet is aged, crooked, weak, and numb.
Thus by enchanting spells I do deceive
Those that behold and look upon my face;
But well may I bid youthful years adieu.

sp.stage: Enter Delia with a pot in her hand
sp.p: See where she comes from whence my sorrows grow! How now, fair Delia! where have you been?

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: At the foot of the rock for running water, and gathering roots for your dinner, sir.

sp.speaker: Sacrapant
sp.p: Ah, Delia, fairer art thou than the running water, yet harder far than steel or adamant!

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: Will it please you to sit down, sir?

sp.speaker: Sacrapant
sp.p: Ay, Delia, sit and ask me what thou wilt, Thou shalt have it brought into thy lap.

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: Then, I pray you, sir, let me have the best meat from the King of England's table, and the best wine in all France, brought in by the veriest knave in all Spain.

sp.speaker: Sacrapant

lg.l: Delia, I am glad to see you so pleasant.
Well, sit thee down. –
Spread, table, spread,
Meat, drink, and bread,
Ever may I have
What I ever crave,
When I am spread,
For meat for my black cock,
And meat for my red.

sp.stage: Enter a Friar with a chine of beef and a pot of wine
sp.p: Here, Delia, will ye fall to?

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: Is this the best meat in England?

sp.speaker: Sacrapant
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: What is it?

sp.speaker: Sacrapant
sp.p: A chine of English beef, meat for a king and a king's followers.

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: Is this the best wine in France?

sp.speaker: Sacrapant
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: What wine is it?

sp.speaker: Sacrapant
sp.p: A cup of neat wine of Orleans, that never came near the brewers in England.

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: Is this the veriest knave in all Spain?

sp.speaker: Sacrapant
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: What is he, a friar?

sp.speaker: Sacrapant
sp.p: Yea, a friar indefinite, and a knave infinite.

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: Then, I pray ye, Sir Friar, tell me before you go, which is the most greediest Englishman?

sp.speaker: Friar
sp.p: The miserable and most covetous usurer.

sp.speaker: Sacrapant
sp.p: Hold thee there, friar. Exit Friar. But soft! Who have we here? Delia, away, begone!

lg.l: Delia, away! for beset are we. –
But heaven nor hell shall rescue her for me.
Brother, was not that Delia did appear,
Or was it but her shadow that was here?
Sister, where art thou? Delia come again!
He calls, that of thy absence doth complain. –
Call out, Calypha, that she may hear,
And cry aloud, for Delia is near.

sp.speaker: Echo
sp.p: Near.

sp.speaker: 1 Brother
sp.p: Near! O, where? Hast thou any tidings?

sp.speaker: Echo
sp.p: Tidings.

sp.speaker: 2 Brother
sp.p: Which way is Delia, then; or that, or this?

sp.speaker: Echo
sp.p: This.

sp.speaker: 1 Brother
sp.p: And may we safely come where Delia is?

sp.speaker: Echo
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: 2 Brother
sp.p: Brother, remember you the white bear of England's wood?

lg.l: "Start not aside for every danger,
Be not afeard of every stranger;
Things that seem are not the same."

sp.speaker: 1 Brother
sp.p: Brother, why do we not, then, courageously enter?

sp.speaker: 2 Brother
sp.p: Then, brother, draw thy sword and follow me.

div1.stage: Enter [Sacrapant] the Conjurer: it lightens and thunders; the 2. Brother falls down.

sp.speaker: 1 Brother
sp.p: What, brother, dost thou fall?

sp.speaker: Sacrapant
sp.p: Ay, and thou too, Calypha. Fall 1. Brother. Enter Two Furies Adeste, dæmones! Away with them:

lg.l: Go carry them straight to Sacrapanto's cell,
There in despair and torture for to dwell.
These are Thenores' sons of Thessaly,
That come to seek Delia their sister forth;
But, with a potion I to her have given,
My arts have made her to forget herself.
lg.stage: He removes a turf, and shows a light in a glass.
lg.l: See here the thing which doth prolong my life.
With this enchantment I do any thing;
And till this fade, my skill shall still endure,
And never none shall break this little glass,
But she that's neither wife, widow, nor maid.
Then cheer thyself; this is thy destiny,
Never to die but by a dead man's hand.

div1.stage: Enter Eumenides, the wandering knight, and [Erestus] the old man at the cross

sp.speaker: Eumenides

lg.l: Tell me, Time,
Tell me, just Time, when shall I Delia see?
When shall I see the loadstar of my life?
When shall my wand'ring course end with her sight,
Or I but view my hope, my heart's delight?

sp.p: [Seeing Erestus] Father, God speed! If you tell fortunes, I pray, good father, tell me mine.

lg.l: Son, I do see in thy face
Thy blessed fortune work apace.
I do perceive that thou hast wit;
Beg of thy fate to govern it,
For wisdom govern'd by advice,
Makes many fortunate and wise.
Bestow thy alms, give more than all,
Till dead men's bone come at thy call.
Farewell, my son! Dream of no rest,
Till thou repent that thou didst best.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: This man hath left me in a labyrinth:

lg.l: He biddeth me give more than all,
"Till dead men's bones come at thy call";
He biddeth me dream of no rest,
Till I repent that I do best.

div1.stage: Enter Wiggen, Corebus, Churchwarden, and Sexton

sp.speaker: Wiggen
sp.p: You may be ashamed, you whoreson scald Sexton and Churchwarden, if you had any shame in those shameless faces of yours, to let a poor man lie so long above ground unburied. A rot on you all, that have no more compassion of a good fellow when he is gone!

sp.speaker: Churchwarden
sp.p: What, would you have us to bury him, and to answer it ourselves to the parish?

sp.speaker: Sexton
sp.p: Parish me no parishes; pay me my fees, and let the rest run on in the quarter's accounts, and put it down for one of your good deeds, o' God's name! for I am not one that curiously stands upon merits.

sp.speaker: Corebus
sp.p: You whoreson, sodden-headed sheep's-face, shall a good fellow do less service and more honesty to the parish, and will you not, when he is dead, let him have Christmas burial?

sp.speaker: Wiggen
sp.p: Peace, Corebus! As sure as Jack was Jack, the frolic'st franion amongst you, and I, Wiggen, his sweet sworn brother, Jack shall have his funerals, or some of them shall lie on God's dear earth for it, that's once.

sp.speaker: Churchwarden
sp.p: Wiggen, I hope thou wilt do no more than thou dar'st answer.

sp.speaker: Wiggen
sp.p: Sir, sir, dare or dare not, more or less, answer or not answer, do this, or have this.

sp.speaker: Sexton
sp.p: Help, help, help!

div1.stage: Wiggen sets upon the parish with a pike-staff.
Eumenides awakes and comes to them

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Hold thy hands, good fellow.

sp.speaker: Corebus
sp.p: Can you blame him, sir, if he take Jack's part against this shake-rotten parish that will not bury Jack?

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Why, what was that Jack?

sp.speaker: Corebus
sp.p: Who, Jack, sir? Who, our Jack, sir? As good a fellow as ever trod upon neat's-leather.

sp.speaker: Wiggen
sp.p: Look you, sir; he gave fourscore and nineteen mourning gowns to the parish when he died, and because he would not make them up a full hundred, they would not bury him: was not this good dealing?

sp.speaker: Churchwarden
sp.p: O Lord, sir, how he lies! He was not worth a halfpenny, and drunk out every penny; and now his fellows, his drunken companions would have us to bury him at the charge of the parish. An we make many such matches, we may pull down the steeple, sell the bells, and thatch the chancel. He shall lie above ground till he dance a galliard about the church-yard, for Steven Loach.

sp.speaker: Wiggen
sp.p:
Sic argumentaris, Domine Loach: – "an we make many such matches, we may pull down the steeple, sell the bells, and thatch the chancel!" – in good time, sir, and hang yourselves in the bell-ropes, when you have done. Domine opponens, præpono tibi hanc
quæstionem , whether will you have the ground broken or your pates broken first? For one of them shall be done presently, and to begin mine, I'll seal it upon your coxcomb.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Hold thy hands, I pray thee, good fellow; be not too hasty.

sp.speaker: Corebus
sp.p: You capon's face, we shall have you turned out of the parish one of these days, with never a tatter to your arse; then you are in worse taking than Jack.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Faith, and he is bad enough. This fellow does but the part of a friend, to seek to bury his friend. How much will bury him?

sp.speaker: Wiggen
sp.p: Faith, about some fifteen or sixteen shillings will bestow him honestly.

sp.speaker: Sexton
sp.p: Ay, even thereabouts, sir.

p.seg: – and I have left me but one poor three half-pence. Now do I remember the words the old man spake at the cross, "Bestow all thou hast," and this is all, "till dead men's bones comes at thy call."

sp.speaker: Wiggen
sp.p: God, and all good, be with you, sir! [Exit Eumenides.] Nay, you cormorants, I'll bestow one peal of Jack at mine own proper costs and charges.

sp.speaker: Corebus
sp.p: You may thank God the long staff and the bilbo-blade crossed not your coxcomb.– Well, we'll to the church-stile and have a pot, and so trill-lill.

sp.speaker: Churchwarden, Sexton
sp.p: Come, let's go.

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: But, hark you, gammer, methinks this Jack bore a great sway in the parish.

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: O, this Jack was a marvellous fellow! he was but a poor man, but very well beloved. You shall see anon what this Jack will come to.

div1.stage: Enter the Harvest-men singing, with women in their hands

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: Soft! who have we here? Our amorous harvesters.

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: Ay, ay, let us sit still, and let them alone.
sp.stage: Here they begin to sing, the song doubled

lg.l: Lo, here we come a-reaping, a-reaping,
To reap our harvest-fruit!
And thus we pass the year so long,
And never be we mute.

div1.stage: Enter Huanebango and [a little later] Corebus, the clown

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: Soft! who have we here?

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: O, this is a choleric gentleman! All you that love your lives, keep out of the smell of his two-hand sword. Now goes he to the conjurer.

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: Methinks the conjurer should put the fool into a juggling-box.

lg.l: Fee, fa, fum,
Here is the Englishman. –
Conquer him that can, –
Came for his lady bright,
To prove himself a knight,
And win her love in fight.

sp.speaker: Corebus
sp.p: Who-haw, Master Bango, are you here? Hear you, you had best sit down here, and beg an alms with me.

sp.speaker: Huanebango
sp.p: Hence, base cullion! Here is he that commandeth ingress and egress with his weapon, and will enter at his voluntary, whosoever saith no.

div1.stage: A voice and flame of fire; Huanebango falleth down

sp.speaker: Voice
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: So with that they kissed, and spoiled the edge of as good a two-hand sword as ever God put life in. Now goes Corebus in, spite of the conjurer.

div1.stage: Enter [Sacrapant] the Conjurer and [Two Furies and] strike Corebus blind

lg.l: Away with him into the open fields,
To be a ravening prey to crows and kites:
lg.stage: [Huanabengo is carried out by the Two Furies.]
lg.l: And for this villain, let him wander up and down,
In naught but darkness and eternal night.
Here hast thou slain Huan, a slashing knight,
And robbed poor Corebus of his sight.
Hence, villain, hence! – Now I have unto Delia
Given a potion of forgetfulness,
That, when she comes, she shall not know her brothers.
Lo, where they labour, like to country slaves,
With spade and mattock on this enchanted ground!
Now will I call her by another name;
For never shall she know herself again,
Until that Sacrapant hath breath'd his last.
See where she comes.
Come hither, Delia, take this goad; here hard
At hand two slaves do work and dig for gold:
Gore them with this, and thou shalt have enough.
Good sir, I know not what you mean.

l.seg: She hath forgotten to be Delia,
But not forgot the same she should forget;
But I will change her name.

lg.l: Fair Berecynthia, so this country calls you,
Go ply these strangers, wench; they dig for gold.
O heavens, how
Am I beholding to this fair young man!
But I must ply these strangers to their work:
See where they come.

div1.stage: Enter the Two Brothers in their shirts, with spades, digging

lg.l: O brother, see where Delia is!
O Delia,
Happy are we to see thee here!
What tell you me of Delia, prating swains?
I know no Delia, nor know I what you mean.
Ply you your work, or else you are like to smart.
Why, Delia, know'st thou not thy brothers here?
We come from Thessaly to seek thee forth;
And thou deceiv'st thyself, for thou art Delia.
Yet more of Delia? Then take this, and smart.
What feign you shifts for to defer your labour?
Work, villains, work; it is for gold you dig.
Peace, brother, peace: this vild enchanter
Hath ravish'd Delia of her senses clean,
And she forgets that she is Delia.
Leave, cruel thou, to hurt the miserable. –
Dig, brother, dig, for she is hard as steel.

div1.stage: Here they dig, and descry the light under a little hill.

lg.l: Stay, brother; what hast thou descried?

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: Away, and touch it not; it is something that my lord hath hidden there.

lg.l: Well said ! thou plyest these pioneers well. –
Go get you in, you labouring slaves.
Come, Berecynthia, let us in likewise,
And hear the nightingale record her notes.

div1.stage: Enter Zantippa, the curst daughter, to the Well with a pot in her hand

sp.speaker: Zantippa
sp.p: Now for a husband, house, and home: God send a good one or none, I pray God! My father hath sent me to the well for the water of life, and tells me, if I give fair words, I shall have a husband. Enter [Celanta,] the foul wench, to the Well for water with a pot in her hand But here comes Celanta, my sweet sister. I'll stand by and hear what she says.

sp.speaker: Celanta
sp.p: My father hath sent me to the well for water, and he tells me, if I speak fair, I shall have a husband, and none of the worst. Well, though I am black, I am sure all the world will not forsake me; and, as the old proverb is, though I am black, I am not the devil.

sp.speaker: Zantippa
sp.p: Marry-gup with a murrain, I know wherefore thou speakest that: but go thy ways home as wise as thou cam'st, or I'll set thee home with a wanion.

div1.stage: Here she strikes her pitcher against her sister's, and breaks them both, and goes her way.

sp.speaker: Celanta
sp.p: I think this be the curstest quean in the world. You see what she is, a little fair, but as proud as the devil, and the veriest vixen that lives upon God's earth. Well, I'll let her alone, and go home and get another pitcher, and, for all this, get me to the well for water.

div1.stage: Enter two Furies out of the Conjurer's cell and lays Huanebango by the Well of Life [and then exeunt].
Enter Zantippa with a pitcher to the well.

sp.speaker: Zantippa
sp.p: Once again for a husband; and, in faith, Celanta, I have got the start of you; belike husbands grow by the well-side. Now my father says I must rule my tongue. Why, alas, what am I, then? A woman without a tongue is as a soldier without his weapon. But I'll have my water, and be gone.

div1.stage: Here she offers to dip her pitcher in, and a Head speaks in the well

lg.l: Gently dip, but not too deep,
For fear you make the golden beard to weep.
Fair maiden, white and red,
Stroke me smooth, and comb my head,
And thou shalt have some cockell-bread.

sp.speaker: Zantippa
sp.p: What is this?

lg.l: "Fair maiden, white and red,
Comb me smooth, and stroke my head,
And thou shalt have some cockell-bread"?
"Cockell" callest thou it, boy? Faith, I'll
give you cockell-bread.

div1.stage: She breaks her pitcher upon his Head: then it thunders and lightens; and Huanebango rises up. Huanebango is deaf and cannot hear.

lg.l: Philida, phileridos, pamphilida, florida, flortos:
Dub dub-a-dub, bounce, quoth the guns, with a sulphurous huff-snuff:
Wak'd with a wench, pretty peat, pretty love, and my sweet pretty pigsnie,
Just by thy side shall sit surnamed great Huanebango:
Safe in my arms will I keep thee, threat Mars or thunder Olympus.

p.seg: Foh, what greasy groom have we here? He looks as though he crept out of the backside of the well, and speaks like a drum perish'd at the west end.

lg.l: O, that I might, – but I may not, woe to my destiny therefore! –
Kiss that I clasp! but I cannot. Tell me, my destiny, wherefore?

p.seg: Whoop! now I have my dream.
I'll now set my countenance, and to her in prose, it may be, this rimram-ruff is too rude and encounter.
Laugh, laugh, Zantippa; thou hast thy fortune, a fool and a husband under one.

sp.speaker: Huanebango
sp.p: Truly, sweetheart, as I seem, about some twenty years, the very April of mine age.

p.seg: Why, what a prating ass is this!

lg.l: Her coral lips, her crimson chin,
Her silver teeth so white within,
Her golden locks, her rolling eye,
Her pretty parts, let them go by,
Heigh-ho, hath wounded me,
That I must die this day to see!

sp.speaker: Zantippa
sp.p: By Gogs-bone, thou art a flouting knave. "Her coral lips, her crimson chin"! ka, wilshaw!

sp.speaker: Huanebango
sp.p: True, my own, and my own because mine, and mine because mine, ha, ha! Above a thousand pounds in possibility, and things fitting thy desire in possession.

p.seg: The sot thinks I ask of his lands. Lob be your comfort, and cuckold be your destiny!

sp.speaker: Huanebango
sp.p: True, sweetheart, and will royalize thy progeny with my pedigree.

lg.l: Wretched Eumenides, still unfortunate,
Envied by fortune and forlon by fate,
Here pine and die, wretched Eumenides,
Die in the spring, the April of my age!
Here sit thee down, repent what thou hast done:
I would to God that it were ne'er begun!

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: You are well overtaken, sir.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: You are heartily well met, sir.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Forbear, I say; who is that which pincheth me?

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Trusting in God, good Master Eumenides, that you are in so good health as all your friends were at the making hereof, God give you good morrow, sir! Lack you not a neat, handsome, and cleanly young lad, about the age of fifteen or sixteen years, that can run by your horse, and, for a need, make your mastership's shoes as black as ink? How say you, sir?

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Alas, pretty lad, I know not how to keep myself, and much less a servant, my pretty boy; my state is so bad.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Content yourself, you shall not be so ill a master but I'll be as bad a servant. Tut, sir, I know you, though you know not me. Are not you the man, sir, – deny it if you can, sir, – that came from a strange place in the land of Catita, where Jack-an-apes flies with his tail in his mouth, to seek out a lady as white as snow and as red as blood? Ha, ha! have I touched you now?

p.seg: I think this boy be a spirit.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Tut, are not you the man, sir, – deny it if you can, sir, – that gave all the money you had to the burying of a poor man, and but one three-half-pence left in your purse? Content you, sir, I'll serve you, that is flat.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Well, my lad, since thou art so importunate, I am content to entertain thee, not as a servant, but copartner in my journey. But whither shall we go? for I have not any money more than one bare three-half-pence.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Well, master, content yourself, for if my divination be not out, that shall be spent at the next inn or alehouse we come to: for, master, I know you are passing hungry; therefore I'll go before and provide dinner until that you come; no doubt but you'll come fair and softly after.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Ay, go before; I'll follow thee.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: But do you hear, master? Do you know my name?

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: No, I promise thee, not yet.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Why, I am Jack.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Jack! Why, be it so, then.

div1.stage: Enter the Hostess and Jack, setting meat on the table; and Fiddlers come to play. Eumenides walketh up and down, and will eat no meat.

sp.speaker: Hostess
sp.p: How say you, sir? Do you please to sit down?

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Hostess, I thank you, I have no great stomach.

sp.speaker: Hostess
sp.p: Pray, sir, what is the reason your master is so strange? Doth not this meat please him?

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Yes, hostess, but it is my master's fashion to pay before he eats; therefore, a reckoning, good hostess.

sp.speaker: Hostess
sp.p: Marry, shall you, sir, presently.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Why, Jack, what dost thou mean? Thou knowest I have not any money; therefore, sweet Jack, tell me, what shall I do?

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Well, master, look in your purse.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Why, faith, it is a folly, for I have no money.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Why, look you, master; do so much for me.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: [looking into his purse.] Alas, Jack, my purse is full of money!

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: "Alas," master! does that word belong to this accident? Why, methinks I should have seen you cast away your cloak, and in a bravado danced a galliard round about the chamber. Why, master, your man can teach you more wit than this. [Re-enter Hostess] Come, hostess, cheer up my master.

sp.speaker: Hostess
sp.p: You are heartily welcome; and if it please you to eat of a fat capon, a fairer bird, a finer bird, a sweeter bird, a crisper bird, a neater bird, your worship never eat of.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Thanks, my fine, eloquent hostess.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: But hear you, master, one word by the way. Are you content I shall be halves in all you get in your journey?

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: I am, Jack, here is my hand.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Enough, master, I ask no more.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Come, hostess, receive your money; and I thank you for my good entertain- ment.

sp.speaker: Hostess
sp.p: You are heartily welcome, sir.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Come, Jack, whither go we now?

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Marry, master, to the conjurer's presently.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Content, Jack. – Hostess, farewell.

div1.stage: Enter Corebus [blind], and Celanta, the foul wench, to the Well for water

sp.speaker: Corebus
sp.p: Come, my duck, come: I have now got a wife. Thou art fair, art thou not?

sp.speaker: Celanta
sp.p: My Corebus, the fairest alive; make no doubt of that.

sp.speaker: Corebus
sp.p: Come, wench, are we almost at the well?

sp.speaker: Celanta
sp.p: Ay, Corebus, we are almost at the well now. I'll go fetch some water; sit down while I dip my pitcher in.

lg.l: Gently dip, but not too deep,
For fear you make the golden beard to weep.
lg.stage: A Head comes up with ears of corn, and she combs them in her lap
lg.l: Fair maiden, white and red,
Comb me smooth, and stroke my head,
And thou shalt have some cockell-bread.
Gently dip, but not too deep,
For fear thou make the golden beard to weep.
lg.stage: A [Second] Head comes up full of gold; she combs it into her lap
lg.l: Fair maid, white and red,
Comb me smooth, and stroke my head,
And every hair a sheaf shall be,
And every sheaf a golden tree.

sp.speaker: Celanta
sp.p: O, see, Corebus, I have comb'd a great deal of gold into my lap, and a great deal of corn!

sp.speaker: Corebus
sp.p: Well said, wench! now we shall have just enough. God send us coiners to coin our gold. But come, shall we go home, sweetheart?

sp.speaker: Celanta
sp.p: Nay, come, Corebus, I will lead you.

lg.l: So, Corebus, things have well hit;
Thou hast gotten wealth to mend thy wit.

div1.stage: Enter [the Ghost of] Jack and [Eumenides] the wandering knight

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Come away, master, come.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Go along, Jack, I'll follow thee. Jack, they say it is good to go cross-legged, and say his prayers backward; how sayest thou?

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Tut, never fear, master; let me alone. Here sit you still; speak not a word; and because you shall not be enticed with his enchanting speeches, with this same wool I'll stop your ears: and so, master, sit still, for I must to the conjurer.

div1.stage: Enter [Sacrapant] the Conjurer to the wandering knight

lg.l: How now! What man art thou that sits so sad?
Why dost thou gaze upon these stately trees
Without the leave and will of Sacrapant?
What, not a word but mum? Then, Sacrapant,
Thou art betray'd.
lg.stage: Enter [the Ghost of] Jack invisible, and taketh off Sacrapant's wreath from his head, and his sword out of his hand
lg.l: What hand invades the head of Sacrapant?
What hateful Fury doth envy my happy state?
Then, Sacrapant, these are thy latest days.
Alas, my veins are numb'd, my sinews shrink.
My blood is pierc'd, my breath fleeting away,
And now my timeless date is come to end!
He in whose life his actions hath been so foul,
Now in his death to hell descends his soul.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: O, sir, are you gone? Now I hope we shall have some other coil. – Now, master, how like you this? The conjurer he is dead, and vows never to trouble us more. Now get you to your fair lady, and see what you can do with her. – Alas, he heareth me not all this while; but I will help that.

div1.stage: He pulls the wool out of his ears.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: How now, Jack? What news?

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Here, master, take this sword, and dig with it at the foot of this hill.

div1.stage: He digs, and spies a light [in a glass].

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: How now, Jack? What is this?

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Master, without this the conjurer could do nothing; and so long as this light lasts, so long doth his art endure, and this being out, then doth his art decay.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Why, then, Jack, I will soon put out this light.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Ay, master, how?

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Why, with a stone I'll break the glass, and then blow it out.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: No, master, you may as soon break the smith's anvil as this little vial; nor the biggest blast that ever Boreas blew cannot blow out this little light; but she that is neither maid, wife, nor widow. Master, wind this horn, and see what will happen. He winds the horn. Here enters Venelia, and breaks the glass, and blows out the light, and goeth in again. So, master, how like you this? This is she that ran madding in the woods, his betrothed love that keeps the cross; and now, this light being out, all are restored to their former liberty. And now, master, to the lady that you have so long looked for.

div1.stage: He draweth a curtain, and there Delia sitteth asleep

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: God speed, fair maid, sitting alone, – there is once. God speed, fair maid, – there is twice. God speed, fair maid, – that is thrice.

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: Not so, good sir, for you are by.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Enough, master, she hath spoke; now I will leave her with you.

lg.l: Thou fairest flower of these western parts,
Whose beauty so reflecteth in my sight
As doth a crystal mirror in the sun;
For thy sweet sake I have cross'd the frozen Rhine;
Leaving fair Po, I sail'd up Danuby
As far as Saba, whose enhancing streams
Cuts twixt the Tartars and the Russians;
These have I cross'd for thee, fair Delia:
Then grant me that which I have su'd for long.
Thou gentle knight, whose fortune is so good
To find me out and set my brothers free,
My faith, my heart, my hand I give to thee.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Thanks, gentle madam; but here comes Jack; thank him, for he is the best friend that we have. Enter [the Ghost of] Jack, with a head in his hand How now, Jack! What hast thou there?

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Marry, master, the head of the conjurer.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Why, Jack, that is impossible; he was a young man.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Ah, master, so he deceived them that beheld him! But he was a miserable, old, and crooked man, though to each man's eye he seemed young and fresh; for, master, this conjurer took the shape of the old man that kept the cross, and that old man was in the likeness of the conjurer. But now, master, wind your horn.

div1.stage: He winds his horn. Enter Venelia, the Two Brothers, and [Erestus] he that was at the cross

lg.l: Welcome, Erestus! welcome fair Venelia!
Welcome, Thelea and Calypha both!
Now have I her that I so long have sought;
So saith fair Delia, if we have your consent.
Valiant Eumenides, thou well deservest
To have our favours; so let us rejoice
That by thy means we are at liberty.
Here may we joy each in other's sight,
And this fair lady have her wandering knight.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: So, master, now ye think you have done; but I must have a saying to you. You know you and I were partners, I to have half in all you got.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Why, so thou shalt, Jack.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Why, then, master, draw your sword, part your lady, let me have half of her presently.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Why, I hope, Jack, thou dost but jest. I promised thee half I got, but not half my lady.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: But what else, master? Have you not gotten her? Therefore divide her straight, for I will have half; there is no remedy.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Well, ere I will falsify my word unto my friend, take her all. Here, Jack, I'll give her thee.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Nay, neither more nor less, master, but even just half.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Before I will falsify my faith unto my friend, I will divide her. Jack, thou shalt have half.

sp.speaker: 1 Brother
sp.p: Be not so cruel unto our sister, gentle knight.

sp.speaker: 2 Brother
sp.p: O, spare fair Delia! She deserves np death.

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Content yourselves; my word is passed to him. – Therefore prepare thyself, Delia, for thou must die.

sp.speaker: Delia
sp.p: Then farewell, world! Adieu, Eumenides!

div1.stage: He offers to strike, and [the Ghost of ] Jack stays him

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Stay, master; it is sufficient I have tried your constancy. Do you now remember since you paid for the burying of a poor fellow?

sp.speaker: Eumenides
sp.p: Ay, very well, Jack.

sp.speaker: Jack
sp.p: Then, master, thank that good deed for this good turn; and so God be with you all!

div1.stage: [The Ghost of] Jack leaps down in the ground.

lg.l: Jack, what, art thou gone? Then farewell, Jack! –
Come, brothers, and my beauteous Delia,
Erestus, and thy dear Venelia,
We will to Thessaly with joyful hearts.

sp.speaker: All
sp.p: Agreed: we follow thee and Delia.

div1.stage: Exeunt omnes [except Frolic, Fantastic, and Madge]

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: What, gammer, asleep?

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: By the mass, son, 't is almost day; and my windows shuts at the cock's-crow.

sp.speaker: Frolic
sp.p: Do you hear, gammer? Methinks this Jack bore a great sway amongst them.

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: O, man, this was the ghost of the poor man that they kept such a coil to bury; and that makes him to help the wandering knight so much. But come, let us in: we we will have a cup of ale and a toast this morning, and so depart.

sp.speaker: Fantastic
sp.p: Then you have made an end of your tale, gammer?

sp.speaker: Madge
sp.p: Yes, faith: when this was done, I took a piece of bread and cheese, and came my way; and so shall you have, too, before you go, to your breakfast.
